newsitem.title: GREECE: DEFIANT GREEK FARMERS CAMP OUT BY ROAD BARRICADES.
newsitem.headline: DEFIANT GREEK FARMERS CAMP OUT BY ROAD BARRICADES.

text.p: Greece's national highway evokes images of a rebel stronghold, with farmers huddled under makeshift tents strung between tractors, distributing rations of bread and feta cheese to their "comrades".

Loudspeakers strung among a sea of tractors, blocking road and rail links for 11 days, crank out old communist party songs and farmers stand guard at chained entrances on either side of the highway camp near this central farm town.
Scores of similiar camps have strung up across Greece since the farmers began seizing roads to press their economic demands in a showdown with the socialist government.
"People from villages all across the country have come to the blockades with food, firewood, whatever they can give," said a farmer who has parked his tractor among thousands of others.

Prime Minister Costas Simitis has rejected their demands for higher price supports, cheaper fuel prices and rescheduling of debts. He says everyone must make sacrifices if Greece wants to be an equal player in European Union.

"Why is it that there is never enough to go around when it comes to farmers?" asked a man sitting by a makeshift fire of rubber tyres and tree branches. "I don't know much about the budget, but these demands are not new, we've been asking for them for years."

Farmers say as long as it doesn't rain too often, they are happy to sit it out, playing cards and backgammon. They have moved tables and chairs into the tents, along with photographs and Christmas trees to make the squatter camps more "cozy."

The walls of their "homes" are the sides of tractors, some have generators and hooked up lights and television sets. But white road lines on the "floor" of the tents are a reminder the farmers are in the middle of the national highway.

"No one really wants to be here, we would rather be in our warm homes or drinking a coffee at the local cafeteria," said Andonis Theodoropoulos, a cotton producer. "But I have a family at home I can't afford to feed."
The smell of burning rubber and smoked meat is ever present. Whole fresh lambs are roasted on spits over the fires.
The wives and children join the farmers at night, and the wine and ouzo flow while now and then someone pulls out a guitar or bouzouki and farmers dance around the tractors.
"We want them back home, where they can have a proper meal," said one farmer's wife. "We don't want to spend Christmas like this."
The farmer's children are nearby playing on the tractors. Vaios Sakas, 24, said he wants to continue producing cotton like his father, but worries about his future.
"I don't want these problems when I have a family, it's not worth it." he said.

On either side of the blockades a barren highway stretches for miles with no traffic. Three kilometres (miles) away dozens of lorries are trapped by the blockades, sitting under a thick fog that has covered the region.
Local and foreign drivers impatiently wait for the blockade to end.
"We were held up by the truckers strike in France, then in Italy, now here," Philip Judge from Oxford who was delivering meat to Azerbaijan said. "We are going to miss Christmas with our children."
They sleep in their cabs at nigh. Food and water are scarce and a hot shower too far away by foot. Drivers from Turkey, Bulgaria, Denmark, Germany and England are equally frustrated.
"I understand the farmers' problems, I sympathize, but what has that got to do with us?" said one driver.

They have staged their own protest, lining their trucks along the road blocking farmers from moving between blockades. Every few days locals bring the lorry drivers sandwiches. Some sympathetic farmers deliver water, cheese and bread.
The protest has frozen transport around the country, traffic across the Bulgarian and Turkish borders has ceased, while Greek markets are running out of produce as Christmas approaches.
